chunks: Common microcontrollers and microprocessors. The question: What are some common microcontrollers/microprocessors?
A microcontroller (MCU) is a complete tiny computer on one chip: a processor, program storage, working memory and input/output hardware. It runs one fixed program and sips power.
A microprocessor (MPU) is mainly the processor.
It needs separate memory chips and storage, and it typically runs a full operating system (software such as Linux that juggles many programs).
Picture a studio apartment next to a house. In the studio, the bed, kitchen and bathroom all fit in one room. It is small, cheap to run, and ready at once. That is the MCU.
A house has a separate kitchen, bedrooms and utility connections. It is far roomier, but you must supply and connect each part. That is the MPU.
The line is blurry, since some big studios are roomier than small houses.
Each point is a representative part (values are typical headline numbers; the Pi 4's 4 GB is external DRAM; H743 is STM32H743, RT1062 is i.
MX RT1062, whose point is nudged up for legibility).

The microcontrollers cluster at low clock and kilobyte-scale on-chip RAM; crossover MCUs reach hundreds of MHz with about 1 MB; application processors jump to GHz clocks and gigabytes of external memory.
Microcontroller (MCU): processor, memory and input/output on one chip ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
Microprocessor (MPU): a processor that needs external memory and an operating system. Core: the processor part of a chip, such as Arm Cortex-M for MCUs or Cortex-A for MPUs.
Bit width: how many bits (single 0 seconds and 1 seconds) the processor handles at once. 8-bit parts are simple; 32-bit parts are the workhorse.
Clock speed: ticks per second that pace the chip, in MHz (millions) or GHz (billions). DRAM: bulk working memory in a separate chip, used by MPUs.
The ATmega328P in the Arduino Uno is an 8-bit MCU running at 16 megahertz.
It has 32 KB (kilobytes, thousands of bytes; a byte is 8 bits) of program storage and 2 KB of working memory, and it finishes most instructions in one tick, so about 16 million per second.
A Raspberry Pi 4 uses four Cortex-A72 cores at 1. 5 gigahertz with gigabytes of separate DRAM, running Linux.
Both are computers, but the Pi has millions of times more working memory. That is the whole idea.

"Microcontrollers integrate CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals: AVR like the ATmega328P in Arduino, PIC, the low-power TI MSP430, and above all 32-bit ARM Cortex-M parts like STMicro's STM32, Nordic's nRF52, the RP2040, plus the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth ESP32.
Microprocessors are CPUs needing external DRAM and an OS: Cortex-A chips such as the Raspberry Pi's Broadcom SoC, NXP i. MX, TI Sitara, and x86.
The boundary is blurry, since fast Cortex-M7 MCUs and chips with both A and M cores exist."
